title: AMUNDSEN, Roald. THE SOUTH POLE: an Account of the Norwegian Antarctic Expedition in the “Fram”, 1910 – 1912. Two volume
description: AMUNDSEN, Roald. THE SOUTH POLE: an Account of the Norwegian Antarctic Expedition in the “Fram”, 1910 – 1912. Two volumes, thick octavo, with all maps and plates, traces of pale foxing, very good in the original decorated red cloth, top edges gilt, others uncut. London, John Murray, [December] 1912. First edition in English: second impression. The second impression is scarcer than the first and was probably issued in significantly smaller numbers. Renard and Rosove record details of alterations in the placement of several plates and maps in this impression as against the first edition (these changes are reflected in the newly printed lists of illustrations in each volume). Apart from these revisions to the lists of illustrations and the addition of the publisher’s edition statement on the imprint page the two impressions are identical. title: ARMOUR, James. THE DIGGINGS, THE BUSH, AND MELBOURNE; or, Reminiscences of Three Years’ Wanderings in Victoria.
description: ARMOUR, James. THE DIGGINGS, THE BUSH, AND MELBOURNE; or, Reminiscences of Three Years’ Wanderings in Victoria. Octavo, a little pale foxing, bound with the original yellow wrappers in later quarter morocco. Glasgow, G.D. Mackellar, 1864. Very scarce reminiscences of the Victorian diggings. Armour arrived in Melbourne in September 1852, and headed directly for the Bendigo diggings; three years searching for gold did not make his fortune. His story is characteristic of the less successful diggers, moving into pastoral employment to finance their search for gold. Ferguson, 6119; Wantrup, 423. Estimate $300/500 Illustrated online at invaluable.com

title: BARRINGTON, George. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES, including Botany Bay, Port Jackson, Parramatta, Sydney, and all its
description: BARRINGTON, George. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES, including Botany Bay, Port Jackson, Parramatta, Sydney, and all its dependencies from the original discovery of the island. Octavo, with engraved title with coloured vignette, handcoloured frontispiece and 13 plates, plus an additional four plates, full-page woodcut in-text, a fine copy in recent half calf. London, Printed for M. Jones, 1802. First edition. The first book with handcoloured topographical views of New South Wales. The History was clearly such a success that Jones decided to prepare a ‘prequel’, describing the voyage from England to Botany Bay, for publication in 1803. This elaborate production was originally issued in parts over 1802 and subsequently sold bound up in volume form. The book has “no real relationship with the earlier 1795 ‘Barrington’ Voyage apart from the unauthorised use of his [Barrington’s] name… In fact [it is] largely extracted, more or less verbatim, from David Collins’s two-volume account” (Wantrup). Ferguson, 345. Estimate $1000/1500 Illustrated online at invaluable.com

title: BEANEY. REEVES, C.E. THE QUEEN v.

title: BELCHER, Captain Sir Edward.
description: BELCHER, Captain Sir Edward. NARRATIVE OF THE VOYAGE OF H.M.S. SAMARANG, during the years 1843-46. title: BONWICK, James. WESTERN VICTORIA; ITS GEOGRAPHY, GEOLOGY, AND SOCIAL CONDITION. The Narrative of an Educational Tour in
description: BONWICK, James. WESTERN VICTORIA; ITS GEOGRAPHY, GEOLOGY, AND SOCIAL CONDITION. The Narrative of an Educational Tour in 1857. title: BROWN, Henry Yorke Lyell.
description: BROWN, Henry Yorke Lyell. NORTHERN TERRITORY OF SOUTH AUSTRALIA, NORTH-WESTERN DISTRICT. Reports (Geological and General) resulting from the Explorations Made by the Government Geologist and Staff during 1905. Foolscap folio, two folding maps and three folding plans, two full-page plates and numerous illustrations in the text, original semi-limp cloth, gilt. Adelaide, C.E. title: BURKE AND WILLS COMMISSION. REPORT OF THE COMMISSIONERS appointed to enquire into and report upon the circumstances conn
description: BURKE AND WILLS COMMISSION. REPORT OF THE COMMISSIONERS appointed to enquire into and report upon the circumstances connected with the Sufferings and Death of Robert O’Hara Burke and William John Wills, the Victorian Explorers. Foolscap folio, title page spotted, first two leaves repaired at blank corner, uncut, printed on blue paper, in modern half calf. Melbourne, John Ferres, Government Printer, 1862. The Commission held twelve hearings between 22 November 1861 and 31 January 1862. Their instructions were uncompromising, specifically requiring them to identify the true cause of the “lamentable result” of the expedition, the circumstances which forced Brahe to leave the Coopers Creek depot; and upon whom “rests the grave responsibility” of there being inadequate supplies for the explorers. The Commission apportioned the blame justly between Burke himself, William Wright, and the Exploration Committee of the Royal Society of Victoria. McLaren, 5542; Maria, 35; Wantrup, 167. Estimate $200/400 Illustrated online at invaluable.com

title: BURNEY, James. A CHRONOLOGICAL HISTORY OF THE DISCOVERIES IN THE SOUTH SEA OR PACIFIC OCEAN. Part I. Commencing with an
description: BURNEY, James. A CHRONOLOGICAL HISTORY OF THE DISCOVERIES IN THE SOUTH SEA OR PACIFIC OCEAN. Part I. Commencing with an Account of the earliest Discovery of that Sea by Europeans, And terminating with the Voyage of Sir Francis Drake, in 1579. Illustrated with Charts [Part II. From the Year 1579, to the Year 1620; Part III. From the Year 1620, to the Year 1688; Volume IV. To the Year 1723, including a History of the Buccaneers of America; Volume V. To the Year 1764]. Five volumes, quarto, with 28 engraved charts (17 folding), 13 plates, and six woodcuts in the text, bound in contemporary marbled boards, modern rebacking and recornering in calf, spines mottled, new endpapers. London, Printed by Luke Hansard and sold by G. and W. Nicol, et al., 1803 - 1806 - 1813 -1816 - 1817. First edition of the cornerstone of the study of the discovery of the Pacific. Burney sailed with Cook as lieutenant on his second and third voyages. He commenced this remarkable undertaking so as to present a continuous history of Pacific discovery over the 250 years prior to Cook and his History is designed as a ‘prequel’ to Hawkesworth’s collection of the voyages of Byron, Wallis, Carteret, and Cook. His work was produced in a sympathetic format that allowed his five volumes to stand comfortably next to the eight quartos of Cook. In this “most important general history of early South Sea discoveries containing practically everything of importance on the subject” (Hill), Burney collected Spanish, Dutch, French and English voyages. Many of the voyage accounts published here are otherwise inaccessible and so the History “must always form the basis of historical research for early voyages and discoveries throughout the Pacific” (Hocken). Provenance: King’s Inn Library, Dublin, with their (contemporary) stamp on the verso of each title. Bagnall, 779; Davidson, p. 37; Ferguson, 372; Hill 2, 221; Hocken, pp. 30-34 (with detailed list of contents); Sabin, 9387. Estimate $8000/12,000 Illustrated online at invaluable.com Lot 16. title: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c.
description: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants of that Country. To which are added, some particulars of New Zealand; compiled, by permission, from the Mss. of Lieutenant-Governor King... [together with] AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, from its first Settlement, in January 1788, to August 1801: with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants of that Country. To which are added, some particulars of New Zealand; compiled, by permission, from the Mss. of Lieutenant-Governor King; and an account of a voyage performed by Captain Flinders and Mr Bass; by which the existence of a Strait separating Van Diemen’s Land from the continent of New Holland was ascertained. Abstracted from the Journal of Mr Bass... Vol. II. Two volumes, quarto, containing in total three maps, 23 plates, (three coloured) and eight half-page engravings (two coloured), some toning as usual in the first volume, three leaves spotted, uniformly bound with both half-titles in half calf and marbled boards of the era, one joint opening at foot, small loss to spine. London, Printed by A. Strahan for T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1798 – 1802. First and best editions: an attractive set in uniform contemporary binding, with the natural history plates in colour. Written by Judge Advocate David Collins, who was also Governor Phillip’s Secretary and close friend and adviser, this was the last of the First Fleet journals and the most detailed and painstaking of all descriptions of the voyage and first settlement. The second volume, based almost entirely on the papers of Governor Hunter supplemented by official records and dispatches, is significantly more uncommon than the first volume. It is of great importance, both for its chronicle of later events and for the narratives of voyages and expeditions of discovery undertaken in the intervening years. These include the first printing of Flinders’s log of his northern voyage of 1799 in the Norfolk along the Queensland coast, as well as the inland expeditions of John Price and Henry Hacking that include the first report of the existence of the koala, the earliest recorded sighting of a wombat on mainland Australia and the first report of the discovery of the lyre-bird, which is here described and illustrated in colour for the first time. In particular, this second volume is of high Victorian interest. Through his friend and collaborator, Governor John Hunter, Collins had access to the journal of George Bass. This he reproduces in detail, a fact that is noted on the titlepage of the second volume stating that it included “an account of a voyage performed by Captain Flinders and Mr Bass; by which the existence of a Strait separating Van Diemen’s Land from the continent of New Holland was ascertained. Abstracted from the Journal of Mr. Bass”. This was the only publication of Bass’s journal of the discovery of the strait that bears his name. Ferguson, 263 and 350; Hill 2, 335 (first volume only); Wantrup, 19 and 20. Estimate $15,000/20,000 Illustrated previous page and online at invaluable.com

title: COOK. HAWKESWORTH, John.
description: COOK. HAWKESWORTH, John. AN ACCOUNT OF THE VOYAGES undertaken by order of His Present Majesty for making Discoveries in the Southern Hemisphere and successively performed by Commodore Byron, Captain Carteret, Captain Wallis, and Captain Cook... Three volumes, quarto, 52 engraved plates and charts (some folding), without the rare “Directions for Placing the Cuts and Charts”, very occasional offsetting and toning, several short tears and one plate marked, one text leaf with stained margin, a handsome set in contemporary calf, with original lettering pieces, hinges reinforced, London, W. Strahan and T. Cadell, 1773. An early issue of the first edition of the official account of Cook’s first voyage and the discovery of Eastern Australia. Edited from Cook’s journals by John Hawkesworth, volumes 2 and 3 comprise the account of Cook’s voyage, while the first volume comprises the official accounts of the voyages of Byron, Wallis and Carteret. Although notable now as the official account of Cook’s great voyage, Hawkesworth’s compendium of this series of great voyages represents the highest achievements of eighteenth-century British maritime exploration. Holmes, 5; Sabin, 30934. Estimate $5000/8000 Illustrated online at invaluable.com

title: COOK, James and James KING. A VOYAGE TO THE PACIFIC OCEAN. Undertaken by the Command of His Majesty, For Making Discover
description: COOK, James and James KING. A VOYAGE TO THE PACIFIC OCEAN. Undertaken by the Command of His Majesty, For Making Discoveries in the Northern Hemisphere. Performed under the direction of Captains Cook, Clerke, and Gore, in His Majesty’s Ships the Resolution and Discovery. In the Years 1776, 1777, 1778, 1779, and 1780. Three volumes, quarto, plus separate folio atlas, complete with 87 engraved plates and maps (many folding), intermittent light foxing, several plates with traces of worming in the outer margin repaired (one with 2 pinpricks in image), in contemporary half calf and marbled boards, minor refurbishing, atlas in sympathetic half calf, with early roan label preserved on front board: a fine set. London, Printed by W. and A. Strahan, for G. Nicol and T. Cadell, 1784. First edition of Cook’s third and final voyage in the Resolution and Discovery, 1776 – 1780, to explore the north Pacific in search of the hoped-for North-West passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The results of the third voyage were as comprehensive and conclusive for the north and central Pacific as his first two voyages had been for the south. Apart from determining that the North-West passage was a chimera, charting the Northwest coast of America as far as Alaska, and discovering Christmas Island, on this voyage Cook made what he considered to be his most valuable discovery: the Sandwich, or Hawaiian Islands, where Cook was tragically murdered in February 1779 in a skirmish on the beach. Forbes, 62; Hill 2, 361; Holmes, 47; Sabin, 16250. Estimate $12,000/15,000 Illustrated online at invaluable.com

description: CUNNINGHAM, Peter. TWO YEARS IN NEW SOUTH WALES; a series of letters, comprising sketches of the actual state of society in that colony... His account of the developing distinctiveness of the Australian people is now considered the classic account from the early colonial era and his observations on the unique Australian vocabulary and accent and on the physical characteristics of the Australian-born youth are of great interest. This important First Fleet book, one of the earliest descriptions of Australia, was written when the expedition to settle New Holland was first proposed publicly in 1786-7. The prominent Picadilly bookseller and publisher, John Stockdale, published the work aiming “to present at one view a connected description of the whole country of New Holland” to a public anxious for information on Botany Bay and the proposed thief colony there. The preface and text discuss the transportation of offenders, with an “Introductory Discourse on Banishment” by William Eden, to whom authorship of the whole book was for a long time attributed. Details of the fleet that was preparing to depart are given as well as a comprehensive account of what was known of the east coast of New Holland. The two fine handcoloured maps are highly regarded and show the entire continent as then known, with an inset map of Botany Bay, and a large folding world map with the “passage from England to Botany Bay in New Holland 1787” showing the route the First Fleet would take. Stockdale was exceptionally well-connected in official circles and this and other works that he published in 1786-7 relating to the proposed Botany Bay experiment were almost certainly prepared with official approval. Sydney, The Bulletin Newspaper Company, 1903. The extremely scarce first edition of a classic first book and one of the most important works of the Nationalist period of Australian literature. Championed by many critics and authors over the decades, Furphy’s picaresque depiction of Australian life in the backblocks has come to hold the highest reputation, some even labelling it ‘the great Australian novel’. Furphy and his contemporary, Henry Lawson, are regarded as the pre-eminent exponents of the bush theme in Australian fiction. Furphy began this novel in 1893 and it was finally published by the Bulletin in 1903. It met with a mediocre critical reception and moderate sales and in 1917 the 800 remaining copies were bought up and reissued by Kate Baker, his champion and helper, with a new title-page and an introductory comment by Vance Palmer. This second issue is comparatively common, whereas the first edition, because few were sold and fewer still treasured, is now an extremely scarce book indeed. title: HOPE, Alec Derwent. DUNCIAD MINIMUS An heroic poem by A.D. Hope Profusely annotated by A.A.P. and A.P. Quarto, [2] + 66
description: HOPE, Alec Derwent. DUNCIAD MINIMUS An heroic poem by A.D. Hope Profusely annotated by A.A.P. and A.P. Quarto, [2] + 66 + 8 leaves typescript, loose in amateur brown paper wrappers (spine fold gone). Melbourne, 1950 [but later]. One of the contemporary typescripts of this notable satire, first written by Hope in a burst of creative energy in 1950 and subsequently revised by him in the early 1960s. Although small portions of the original 1950 version were published in local literary magazines, the complete 1950 work is known only as this scribal publication, typed on several manual typewriters with their associated carbon copies. A satirical attack on fellow critic, A.A. Phillips, the Dunciad Minimus was a private joke, not intended for publication, and distributed in limited numbers to fellow academics at the University of Melbourne, who proceeded to lend it to others and have typescript and carbon tyescript copies made. The present piece is one of those rare unofficial scribal ‘publications’. In 1963 the Dunciad was printed by Hope’s own department at the Australian National University as a processed typescript and distributed privately. That Canberra printing is rare, as are examples of the earlier typescripts of the 1950s. Apart from these typescripts, of which very few are known, and the Canberra printing, of which again few are known, there is no author’s manuscript extant. A fully revised edition was published in 1970 by Melbourne University Press as Dunciad Minor: An heroick poem. Also in the lot is another later (1960s?) transcript of the pre-1963 text, the copy text typed on an electric typewriter (Quarto, [2] + 66 + 8 leaves typescript, string-bound in a plain manilla folder). From the collection of the late Professor John Barnes; most survinging copies of the 1950s and 1963 ‘editions’ have academic associations. Estimate $500/800 Illustrated online at invaluable.com

Minns), pale shadow on part of title page, an attractive copy in original wrappers, the staples rusting: signed in pencil by Jim Tyrrell, and with his Lionel Lindsay bookplate on the rear wrapper. Sydney, Louisa Lawson, 1894. The first and only edition of the first book by a great Australian writer, printed and published by his mother, an outstanding early Australian feminist who employed only women for her printing and publishing ventures. The volume was itself a nationalistic statement: “an attempt to publish, in Australia, a collection of sketches and stories at a time when everything Australian... must bear the imprint of a London publishing firm before our critics will condescend to notice it”. But in the end Lawson was unhappy with the book and his inscription in David Scott Mitchell’s copy reads: “This is my first book. Only a few copies were published fortunately. I withdrew the book from publication. The book should be interesting as a curiosity in printing”. Despite this self-deprecating tone, some of Lawson’s best-known and most enduring work was printed here, including “The Drover’s Wife” and “The Union Buries its Dead”. title: MANN, Leonard. FLESH IN ARMOUR. A Novel.
description: MANN, Leonard. FLESH IN ARMOUR. A Novel. Octavo, very good in original cloth with typographical dustwrapper. Melbourne, Phaedrus, 1932. “Le grand classique du roman de guerre Australien” (Jean François Vernay). First edition: complete with the rarely seen dustwrapper. Mann’s self-published first novel, winner of the 1932 Australian Literature Society gold medal. Mann fought with the infantry on the Western Front and was injured at Passchendaele. In the late 1920s, he was asked to write the history of his battalion. Instead he wrote Flesh in Armour. A novel based closely on his experiences on and off the battlefield, Flesh in Armour is marked out from other Australian fiction of the war by its uncompromising realism. Mann was not writing a book to be part of the great commemorative and mythopoeic programme begun by C.E.W. Bean but one to honour his comrades by its honesty and realism, by its truthful depiction of the horrors of trench warfare contrasted with the adventures and comic highlights of life off the battlefield. It is this frank realism that still has the power to confront and surprise modern readers. One is not shocked by encounters with the prostitutes of London and Le Havre, nor by openness about crudity, mutiny, suicide, and disillusion, not by his contempt for the comically – but fatally – incompetent and insouciant British officers, nor by caustic ridicule of English high society. But one is shocked that a writer in 1932 should have written so forthrightly against the prevailing commemorative stream. It was this aspect of Flesh in Armour that so disturbed many contemporary readers and publishers. Not returned servicemen, however, who appear fairly uniformly to have admired it. title: SLESSOR, Kenneth. THIEF OF THE MOON. Folio in sixes, 40 leaves in seven unsigned folio gatherings (i.e.
description: SLESSOR, Kenneth. THIEF OF THE MOON. Folio in sixes, 40 leaves in seven unsigned folio gatherings (i.e. [AF]6, [G]4), eccentrically paginated pp. [4] (front pastedown and free endpaper), [xii] (engravings tipped onto pp. [vi] and [xii], 1 – 39, [40] (blank), [2] (recto text, verso with tipped on engraving), 40[bis] (recto) – [45] (verso), 45[bis] – [54] (last blank), [2] (blank), [4] (back free endpaper and pastedown), with three mounted numbered engravings by Norman Lindsay, original quarter white calf and leather-grain blue-green cloth boards, the spine lettered and ruled in gilt, top edge gilt, others uncut, with the rare dustwrapper, with paper label on the spine panel and overlapping edges. Sydney, Hand-press of J.T. Kirtley, 1924. Rare: a beautiful copy of Slessor’s first published work with a rare suite of Norman Lindsay’s engravings. Number 10 of an edition purporting to be limited to 130 copies signed by the author. Although all proposed copies of the text were actually printed and bound, John Kirtley has several times recorded that at least half the edition was destroyed by a fire in the warehouse where the bound copies were stored. A similar reduction was suffered to the edition of Jack Lindsay’s Fauns and Ladies but a more substantial number of copies of Lindsay’s book had been distributed before the blaze. Of the surviving copies not many seem to have been distributed after the fire because Lindsay and Kirtley packed up and left for England soon after, taking with them the remaining bound copies. These bound copies were technically incomplete because, while Norman Lindsay had produced the requisite number of signed and numbered wood-engravings, these had not all been tipped into their respective volumes. That chore was left until copies were actually despatched to buyers (the same was true of Fauns and Ladies). Accordingly, a substantial number of the 60 or 70 copies extant were never finished and never properly issued. Taking into account the loss of half the edition by fire, and the fact that a substantial portion of the copies that survived the fire were never completed and never issued, it is possible to estimate that perhaps only between about 30 and 50 complete copies were ever distributed and certainly no more than about 70. Thief of the Moon, complete with the Norman Lindsay wood-engravings, is one of the more manifestly rare ‘first books’ by a major Australian writer. Arnold, Fanfrolio Press (2009), 2 (suggesting that perhaps only a third of the edition was made up); Miller, p. 334; People, Print & Paper, 179; Serle, p. 184; Cains, 159. Estimate $2800/4200 Illustrated online at invaluable.com
